questions.q: What problem does Infrastructure as Code solve compared to manually clicking through a cloud portal?
options: It eliminates the need for cloud providers entirely
It requires no configuration files at all
It makes infrastructure changes repeatable, version-controlled, and reviewable as code, rather than undocumented manual clicks
It only works for on-premises hardware
questions.explain: IaC turns infrastructure changes into code that can be diffed, reviewed in a pull request, and re-applied consistently, instead of relying on someone remembering exactly which portal buttons they clicked.

questions.q: What's a fundamental difference between Terraform and Bicep?
options: Terraform is Azure-only while Bicep works across multiple clouds
Bicep requires a separate state file per resource while Terraform needs none
They are two names for the exact same tool
Terraform is a multi-cloud tool with its own HCL language and state file, using providers to talk to different clouds; Bicep is an Azure-native DSL that transpiles down to ARM JSON templates
questions.explain: Terraform's provider model lets one tool and language target Azure, AWS, GCP, and more, tracked via its own state file. Bicep is scoped to Azure specifically and compiles into ARM templates, which Azure Resource Manager then deploys.

questions.q: In Terraform, what is a "provider"?
options: A plugin that lets Terraform manage resources for a specific platform (e.g. azurerm for Azure, aws for AWS) by translating HCL resource blocks into API calls
A person who supplies cloud credentials
A section of the state file that lists outputs
A Bicep-only concept
questions.explain: Providers are the plugins that know how to talk to a given platform's API. Declaring the azurerm provider is what lets a resource block like azurerm_storage_account actually get created in Azure.

questions.q: Why does Terraform maintain a "state" file?
options: To store a cached copy of documentation
To store the provider's source code
It does not maintain any state
To track which real-world resources correspond to which resource blocks in configuration, so Terraform knows what to create, update, or destroy on the next apply
questions.explain: State is Terraform's record of what it believes exists and how it maps to your configuration. Without it, Terraform would have no way to know whether a resource block describes something already provisioned or something new.

questions.q: What's a risk of manually editing a resource that Terraform manages, outside of Terraform?
options: There is no risk; Terraform automatically ignores manual changes
It causes "drift" between the real infrastructure and Terraform's recorded state, which Terraform will detect and try to reconcile (often by overwriting the manual change) on the next apply
It automatically rewrites the .tf configuration files to match
It permanently locks the resource from any further changes
questions.explain: Terraform compares real infrastructure against its state on each run. A manual, out-of-band change creates drift, and the next plan/apply will typically propose reverting it back to match the configuration unless the config is updated to match reality.

questions.q: What does a Terraform resource block declare?
options: A variable's default value
A single infrastructure object to create and manage, identified by a resource type and a local name, along with its configuration arguments
An output value only
A provider's version constraint
questions.explain: A resource block (e.g. resource "azurerm_storage_account" "main" { ... }) is the core unit of Terraform configuration — it says "this specific object should exist with these settings."

questions.q: What's the difference between a Terraform variable and an output?
options: They are functionally identical in Terraform
Variables can only hold strings; outputs can only hold numbers
Outputs are set before apply and variables are set afterward
A variable is a parameterized input to a configuration; an output exposes a value (often computed, like a resource's generated ID) after apply for other configs or the CLI to consume
questions.explain: Variables parameterize a configuration so the same code can be reused with different inputs. Outputs surface results — frequently attributes only known after resources are created, like a storage account's connection string or an ID.

questions.q: When provisioning an Azure Storage Account with Terraform, which attribute is essential and generally forces resource recreation if you try to change it after the fact?
options: The tags block
The access_tier setting
The storage account name, which is globally unique and tied to its DNS endpoint
The description field
questions.explain: A storage account's name becomes part of its public DNS endpoint (accountname.blob.core.windows.net) and must be globally unique across Azure, so it can't simply be edited in place — changing it means creating a new account.

questions.q: What is a Terraform module primarily used for?
options: Storing Terraform's binary executable
Replacing the need for providers
Encapsulating and reusing a group of resources with a defined set of inputs and outputs, so the same infrastructure pattern can be provisioned repeatedly
A synonym for a single resource block
questions.explain: Modules let teams package a proven pattern (say, "a storage account plus its private endpoint and access policies") behind a small set of inputs, so it can be reused across environments instead of copy-pasting resource blocks.

questions.q: What does terraform plan do that terraform apply does not?
options: It applies changes without asking for confirmation
It deletes the state file
It rewrites the provider's source code
It shows a preview of what actions Terraform would take (create, update, or destroy) to reconcile state with configuration, without making any actual changes
questions.explain: plan is a dry run: it computes the diff between desired configuration and current state and shows exactly what would change, letting you review before anything is actually created or destroyed.

questions.q: Provisioning an Azure Event Hub, which setting most directly determines how many consumers can read from the stream in parallel?
options: The number of partitions on the Event Hub
The resource group's location
The provider's version pin
The default value on a variable block
questions.explain: Partitions are Event Hubs' unit of parallelism — each partition can be read by only one consumer within a consumer group at a time, so partition count caps how much a single consumer group can parallelize reads.

questions.q: What is Bicep, technically?
options: A general-purpose programming language for building applications
A domain-specific language that compiles (transpiles) down to ARM JSON templates for deploying Azure resources
A NoSQL database product
An alternative to the Azure Portal with no relation to ARM
questions.explain: Bicep is a declarative DSL purpose-built for Azure deployments. Every Bicep file compiles down to the same ARM JSON template format that Azure Resource Manager has always consumed — it's a friendlier authoring layer on top of ARM, not a replacement for it.

questions.q: In a Bicep file, what's the difference between a param and a var?
options: They behave identically in every respect
param declares an input supplied at deployment time (optionally with a default); var declares a value computed or derived within the template itself
var is only for secrets, while param is for everything else
param can only hold numeric values
questions.explain: Parameters are the template's external interface — values the caller supplies at deploy time. Variables are internal helpers computed from expressions inside the template and aren't meant to be set externally.

questions.q: When deploying an Azure SQL setup in Bicep with a sqlServer resource containing a nested database sub-resource, what does that nesting express?
options: Nothing; nesting in Bicep is purely cosmetic
A random ordering with no real meaning
The dependency and containment relationship, so the database is provisioned as a child of that specific logical SQL server
An unrelated storage hierarchy
questions.explain: Nesting a resource inside another in Bicep expresses a parent-child relationship (like a database belonging to a specific server), and Bicep uses that to infer both the correct resource ID scoping and the deployment order dependency.

questions.q: What's the main advantage Bicep offers over hand-written ARM JSON templates?
options: ARM templates deploy noticeably faster than Bicep templates
Bicep has no relationship to ARM whatsoever
Bicep provides simpler, more readable syntax — no giant nested JSON, native loops and conditionals — while still compiling to the exact same underlying ARM templates and deployment engine
Bicep replaces the need for resource providers
questions.explain: Bicep exists specifically to make ARM deployments easier to author and read; it doesn't change what Azure actually deploys underneath, since it compiles straight to ARM JSON before the ARM deployment engine ever sees it.

questions.q: What does deploying a Bicep file at resource-group scope actually trigger, from Azure's perspective?
options: A Terraform state file gets created
An ARM deployment that Azure Resource Manager processes just like a submitted ARM JSON template
A Kubernetes manifest apply
A brand-new Azure subscription
questions.explain: Bicep is compiled to ARM JSON before deployment, and Azure Resource Manager processes that compiled template through its normal deployment pipeline — Bicep is a client-side authoring convenience, not a separate deployment mechanism.

questions.q: Why is storing Terraform state remotely (e.g. in an Azure Storage Account backend) preferred over a local state file for team use?
options: Remote state offers no benefit over local state for a team
It makes Terraform run without needing any provider
It eliminates the need to ever run terraform plan
It enables locking to prevent concurrent applies from corrupting state, and gives the whole team a single shared source of truth
questions.explain: A local state file lives on one person's machine and can't be safely shared; a remote backend with locking ensures two people (or two pipeline runs) can't apply changes against the same state simultaneously and corrupt it.

questions.q: What is the purpose of terraform import (or the equivalent import tooling for Bicep/ARM)?
options: To delete a resource permanently
To bring a resource that already exists in the cloud, but was created outside of IaC, under management by associating it with a resource block and state entry
To duplicate a resource automatically across regions
To convert Terraform code into Bicep code
questions.explain: Import doesn't create anything new — it links an existing real-world resource to a configuration block so that tool can start managing (and diffing against) something a human previously created by hand.

questions.q: In a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure as code, what's a common, safe pattern for pull requests?
options: Automatically run apply/deploy directly against production on every commit with no review
Skip planning entirely and go straight to apply
Store the cloud credentials directly in the pull request description for convenience
Run plan (or what-if for Bicep/ARM) on the pull request to show the proposed changes, and only run apply/deploy after human review and merge
questions.explain: Surfacing the plan/what-if output as a PR check lets reviewers see exactly what infrastructure will change before it happens, catching unintended deletions or costly changes before they ever reach apply.

questions.q: Why does the plan/apply (or what-if/deploy) workflow exist as two separate steps rather than one combined step?
options: It has no real purpose besides slowing deployments down
Plan (or what-if) modifies real infrastructure just like apply does
It lets you preview and review exactly what will change before committing to a possibly destructive action
Apply is optional and never actually required to make changes take effect
questions.explain: Separating the read-only preview from the actual mutating step is a deliberate safety mechanism — it gives a human (or an automated policy check) a chance to catch a destructive or unexpected change before it's irreversibly applied.
